text: folks could go ahead and take their seats. We are starting two or three minutes late, but I want to get us started. I know there are still people filing in, having conversations, but we have time until 4.30 today. I want to make sure we maximize that time to the extent possible.

I'm going to kick off this meeting, February 24th, budget committee meeting, joint budget committee meeting with our school board, and just a few high-level things. We're going to let staff get through all their presentations, and then we're going to have a chance for everybody to ask a question. I'm going to encourage everybody, given the large number of people that are here, to ask questions. If you want to give some comments before your question, that's fine, but try to limit those and focus on questions at this session, because obviously we're going to get a presentation on the budget and want to make sure everyone in this room who's on the school

board or county board has a chance to ask those questions. Before we get started, I do want to thank our colleagues from the school board for joining us. Thank our budget staff, county budget staff, and school budget staff. As you'll see in this presentation, they work on these budgets all year long. They collaborate all year long. And so while we're here for an hour and a half, they are constantly working on this. And I also want to point out that we're in a year that we know faces a lot of challenges. I appreciate that both our school system has put forward a budget

that's within reason and that our county executive has put forward a budget that follows the board's guidance from last year and recognizes the somewhat unusual financial situation that we find ourselves in with so much happening at the federal level and so many other challenges that our families are facing, and keeping in mind their ability to pay and be able to afford to live in the county, I know was a driver in the work that was done to get us to this point on both budgets. Obviously, public education is our highest priority in the county, as you can see in

the budget, clearly identified again this year. And I'll make some closing comments when we're finished, but I think another obvious thing to point out here is there is a small gap between what has been requested by the school system and what is in the county executive's proposed budget, and I'm going to speak for myself here, but I think I'm probably speaking for many, that we hope our friends in Richmond are aggressively filling that gap. We know that, you know, so much of our budget challenges when it comes to public education begin there, and we're seeing some promising signs in Richmond that there'll be some strides made and some gains

made this year and adequately funding public education in the Commonwealth of Virginia so that that's not continually borne on the backs of real estate tax bills in Fairfax County and something that we're working on. And then finally, because this question came up before, as you'll see in the budget presentation, the total amount of the meals tax is already included in the budget.

And as we heard, as the county executive presented his budget to us, without that meals tax, we would not be looking at a budget that has been proposed by the county executive that keeps the tax rate flat. And we know that a flat tax rate still equates to an increase in taxes for people based on assessment, but without that meals tax, we would be having a totally different conversation, but that is already baked into the numbers. And so I'm going to leave the rest for our county staff, but before I turn to them, I'm going to turn to my partner, the chair of the school board, Sandy Anderson, if you would like to offer some opening comments. I just wanted to say thank

again for the opportunity for us all to come and speak with you. I think that it's important for us to have those moments where we share the questions and that we hear what everybody's thinking, so I am always grateful for the opportunity for us to come talk. Thank you very much, Ms. Anderson, for that, and look forward to that conversation, and to get us started, I'm going to turn over to, first, I'm going to ask our county executive if there's any comments he wants to make, and then we're going to turn to budget staff to give us our presentation. No, I'm just going to say welcome to everybody here today and turn it over to anything you want to say?

To Christina. Christina Jackson. Christina Jackson, who is our Chief Financial Officer. Welcome. Good afternoon, everyone. Once again, I'm joined by my counterpart at the schools, Lee Burden, as well as the county's budget director, Phil Hagen, and the school's budget director, Alice Wigington.

So the presentation that we have for you guys today is very brief. Certainly the full presentations that were provided by both the county and the schools are available online, so our intention this afternoon is to kind of hit the high points. So on the first slide, this is just an overview of the county's advertised budget. As the chairman mentioned, our proposed budget is based on the current real estate tax rate of $1.12 and a quarter, which does equate to an increase for the average homeowner of about $357, based on an almost 4% increase in residential assessments.

It does recognize the full year impact of the food and beverage tax, which does include an increase in this year's budget of about $68 million. It provides $118 million in additional support for the schools. We have a little bit more information on that later regarding the breakout of what's operating, capital construction and debt service. It does partially fund the superintendent's request with a shortfall of about $44 million. We've noted in here that when you combine this $118 million increase in the transfers, as well as some of the flexibility

provided in the former governor's budget, both in terms of increased revenue as well as a reduction in the Virginia retirement system employee contribution rate that equated to flexibility in the school's budget of over $200 million. On the county side, we have funded our county's compensation program. You'll see a real focus in the county's budget on capital renewal. We know that's a need for the schools as well, and we've included funding for that. We have included about $32.9 million in reductions. This is the fourth year that we've included reductions on the county side, and that includes 107 merit positions.

As well, there's a balance of about $23 million. That's about average of what we've had in balance over the past five years ago. It certainly has fluctuated, and we do have some funds identified separately in reserve, both for some potential loss in urban area security initiatives funding, as well as our reserve for economic uncertainty.

When we move to the next slide, this is an overview of both the county and school's revenues. I'll cover the chart on the left really quickly. Real estate, you can see that we're estimating about $133 million in additional revenue. We do have more detail on the real estate components on the next slide.

We've got about a 3.1% increase in personal property. That's based on an increase both in the number of vehicles as well as the average value of those vehicles for the next year based on January values. We have a small increase in local sales tax, and then you can see that almost $68 million for food and beverage tax.
representing the second six months of the four-year impact. So in total, county revenues are projected to increase just under $270 million. Good afternoon.

Again, I'm Lee Burden, CFO for the schools. On the school's revenue side, this represents the superintendent's proposed budget. The county transfer request is $138.45 million, and it's worth noting again that that's about half of our request at this same time last year.

Sales tax and state aid, up $71 million. That's largely due to the local composite index reduction, as well as re-benchmarking and assumption of a 2% comp increase. Federal revenue, of course, we're assuming that's flat. And the beginning balance and other revenue is changes to the beginning balance offset by Fairfax tuition for a total projected revenue increase of $197 million.

Our next slide includes our chart, which provides more detail on changes in our real estate tax base. We've included both a breakout for residential and non-residential values. And you can see that first-line residential equalization is projected to increase by 3.99%.

So we've seen resilience in our residential market. Certainly that is a slight decrease over the appreciation that we saw last year. The value of a penny in FY27 is about $35 million to the county in terms of revenue. The impact on the homeowner of that penny is about $83, just kind of for information.

We were happy to see, therefore, non-residential equalization that we were positive at 0.92%. That's the first time in three years that we've been positive in non-residential equalization. And we also saw the office vacancy rate decrease for the first time since 2019. And so we're hopeful that maybe we've turned a corner with commercial values.

Certainly, we're going to be keeping an eye on that. But certainly, we've seen obsolete office space be demolished. there's no speculative office construction right now. The small amount of office construction that is occurring has all been leased and is expected to be fully occupied. So we're hopeful that those factors are going to contribute to continued positive trends on the commercial side. Both in total, our real estate tax base is projected to increase by 3.77% for next year. This next slide is kind of where we'll probably spend the most time. These are just the numbers kind of behind

our respective budget proposals. We have split out the school's information a little bit differently this year just because there was a lot going on and we wanted to make sure that we were clear in what was included in the proposed budget. Those first couple of lines include the increased county revenues, so that $270 million kind of as it's kind of divided up both on the county side and the school side. I will note that you see that there's a reduction of about $6.5 million off to the right, which is related to our increase in the transient occupancy tax last year that's

being redirected to visit Fairfax. So last year we brought it in and held it in balance. This year we're going to be directly posting it to our contributory fund. So it's kind of taken out of the general fund, but it's net zero for purposes of this discussion. We have included the school operating transfer of 94.6%. That's kind of the pure operating transfer increase. In addition, we've included about $4.6 million in operating transfer increase related to programs that we are proposing get shifted over to schools. We've included $11.4 million for school debt service.

That's related really to two things. One is an increase in interest rates and also the fact that we are selling more in bonds now than we were 20 years ago. And so the debt that's falling off from 20 years ago was certainly a nod at the $230 million that we're selling for schools now on an annual basis. And then we've included $7.5 million for the school's construction fund. This is in line with the $2.5 million that we proposed a number of years ago following the joint CIP school county CIP committee, where we had recommended getting to a full penny on the

real estate tax base in combination of the increased debt service related to our increased bond sales and in additional capital renewal funding, so PAGO funding in both the county and schools. So this $7.5 million for schools is matched on the county side. So now we have achieved the $10 million in the base for both the county and schools. And I will note that we are also now over the one penny on the real estate tax rates. We actually have fulfilled all of the recommendations that came from that committee back in 2021. And then I'll quickly go down the county requirements. Again, I noted the compensation, the pay and benefits number for the county. It's

about $102 million. That does fully fund all of the county's collective bargaining agreements, as well as commensurate increases for our non-represented employees, as well as some increases for health insurance and retirement. Our $7.42 million is related to the county's debt service increases. Then you can see we have 12 and a half again for capital renewal.

Certainly we know this is again a challenge for both the county and the schools, but you'll see that we have some significant investments on the county side for capital renewal. And we also propose some changes in our bond program as well as it relates to some of our facilities. You can see that $4.59 million decrease on the county side. And again, the positive on the school side is we're proposing to transfer programs to schools. That's primarily related to the middle school after school program. Then some of those other priorities, that 61.45 is related to inflationary adjustments, IT spending. We did have some increased dollars to help our most vulnerable

residents in terms of rental assistance and food assistance. So that's baked into that 61 million dollars. And then we did have reductions of almost 33 million dollars and that's 107 positions that I mentioned earlier and all of those reductions are detailed in our budget package. And so now I'll turn it over to Lee to cover kind of the school's side of the equation.

Yeah. Again, the revenue piece just represents what the county's executive's advertised budget proposes, which is $94.6 million for the schools in increased county transfer. The additional school's revenue is all other funding sources, the federal, the beginning balance, and other, and state combined.

And as far as our requirements go, the compensation pay and benefits honors our collective bargaining agreements, as well as includes a reduction for the pension plan that BRS initiated and increases in health care costs.

The other priorities are some very slight multi-year investments, contractual increases and baseline adjustments. And the 35.71 reduction for school enrollment is a reduction of 260 FTEs based on the rerun of the enrollment.

So that at least for the school operating fund, we're looking at a $43.8 million gap, assuming that the programs transferred to school operating and the school construction are allocated for the purposes that the county executive budget assumes.

The next slide we've included really just for information, because we've typically included this chart in this presentation. These are the pay adjustments for both the county and the schools over the past three years. Some of the categories have changed from our traditional presentation. That's really just, you know, and jointly talking with the school staff, you know, with collective bargaining, some of those groupings have changed a little bit. So the history doesn't go back quite as far as we would normally share, but that's only because it's kind of more difficult since kind of those groupings are a little bit different. So we've provided the last three years and we've noted on this chart where the collective bargaining went into effect. So for example, for

the county's public safety, it's the full three-year period where for the school's principals and administrators, it's just FY27. So again, this is just informational. We weren't planning on spending a lot of time on this chart. The next slide, again, is informational. This is our budget timeline. I think that, you know, the key dates coming up are the school board adopting their advertised budget just in a couple of days, and our board of supervisors taking action to advertise FY27 tax rates on March 17th, but we have all of our information here related to our public hearings and our budget adoption dates. Did you have anything that you wanted to share?

And so then our last slide, Philly, is looking ahead kind of for the remainder of this fiscal year as well as when we look ahead to FY2028. You know, certainly we're going to continue to monitor our revenues, particularly the food and beverage tax.

The first deadline for that was just last week. We're anticipating on an average month that we would receive a little bit over $11 million. What we've received so far is a little bit over $9 million. Certainly some of that could be seasonality. That could be impacted by the storm. We also know that there are some businesses that are continuing to come online, and so we're going to be continuing to monitor that to see if we need to make any adjustments to our food and beverage tax revenue projections.

We do have two upcoming budget committees over the next few weeks, on March 10th and 24th. And then as we look ahead to FY28, you know, I know sometimes it feels like a little bit like we're a broken record that we say every year is going to be a difficult budget year. But as we look ahead to 28, we're seeing a softening in the residential market and some of our surrounding jurisdictions.

so certainly that's something that we will be monitoring closely. Again, as I noted earlier, we are optimistic about the commercial market, so we're hopeful that that continues to trend in a positive direction. On the county side, we will be renegotiating our two public safety collective bargaining agreements coming up actually in the next few weeks, and those will be impacting the FY28 budget.

We do anticipate increasing retirement and health contributions for next year, Particularly on the retirement side, which impacts both the county and the schools, we are performing a five-year experience study, and so we anticipate that that's going to have upward pressure on our employer contribution rates for all three of our retirement systems.

We anticipate increased debt service based on some anticipated bond sales, particularly EDA bond sales, continued operating growth, and then certainly on the transportation side, although we're hopeful that the state is going to come forward with some additional transportation funding, We'll also be keeping an eye on that to see how that might impact our FY28 budget.

That's it again. We need to go through it quickly and make sure that you guys have plenty of time for your questions. We appreciate that. Thank you all for that presentation. And we're going to go around and ask questions. If we have time for a second round, we'll certainly take advantage of that.

But let me start with Ms. Anderson to see if she has any questions, and then we'll make our way around the table in this order. And if we have time for a second round, we'll do that. I don't have any questions. I've been spending a lot of time rolling around in numbers for the last couple weeks.

But what I will say is that I want us all to remember, or that I firmly remember, that when we're talking about the delta between what we need and what we're talking about getting, I fully and completely understand that that number is in addition to the $3 billion that the county is dedicated to our schools.

So I just want to make sure that we're level setting that conversation, that when we're talking about the Delta, it's a tiny little percentage of where we need to go. And what I've been saying all along is we are at the tipping point moment where we need help from the state.

We no longer can sustain the education level in this county purely with taxpayer money, like from property taxes. It's just not going to work. And so I am hopeful, but as my husband likes to tell me, hope is not a method. So we need to continue with our counterparts in Richmond and be loud about the fact that we need help.

And so I hope that we are able to do that this year. I'm hoping that it's not going to get easier for anybody from here to make these hard decisions. And so I'm really hoping that our governor and our newly installed legislators down there can go ahead and do what needs to be done here to start writing the position that we're in.

So thank you, and I look forward to the conversation. Well said. Thank you. Ms. Dixit? Thank you, everyone. I'm speaking as a budget chair this year, and this position came to me after the size of Heiser got elected.

It just came. I just forgot it. So I'm really thankful for this opportunity for all of us to be in the same room to discuss a very important topic. And FCPS cannot, you know, collect its own funds. We don't have taxing authority.

We do not have our own methods of, you know, making an income. So we depend on others. So one of our funders, our county supervisors, are very thankful for that. Today, we just want to make one point that we thank you for the funds you have given us, but we still have a $43 million gap, and that gap is going to affect somewhere in our staff, in our student population by giving the quality of education could suffer because we are a very heavy, you know, like a labor-intensive, you know, industry.

So we do have to provide a lot of salaries to like 90% of our budget goes to the salaries of our different staff we have. We had a tough last year. We had to wait until the last minute to, you know, make the cuts.

So we are hoping we'll get some answers from the state soon, and then we can make some decisions for our schools, and hopefully we'll get this $43 million from somewhere. Thank you so much. Thank you, Ms. Dixon. All right, very good.

Supervisor Herity. Yeah, I'm going to go a little different direction this year, and for those that watched the board meeting where the budget was introduced last year, I spent a lot of time talking about renovation versus new capital facilities. Just looking at the school population, kind of hit a high in 2022 of $188,799.
In 2025, it kind of rebounded up to $181,700. But in 2027, it's projected to drop 176,133, which is – and it's projected to continue to drop, as I understand.

Somebody can correct me if I'm wrong on that. There's a clear decline in kindergarten, and this is a national trend. This isn't necessarily unique to Fairfax County. But our neighbors in Prince William and Loudoun have stepped back from their capital improvement program and are pausing new school construction.

but we're proposing to build two new schools and we bought a third so I so I'm kind of wondering why we're increasing capacity when we've got a declining population and our neighbors are not so I don't need that answer now but that would be good to get back and whether the increase in operating costs as a result the West well first of all what are the increase in operating costs as a result of the new Western high school I assume there's going to be a new principal a new set of administration new facilities folks and that sort of thing so that's those are the two questions kind of generally and

I'm asking these questions on the county side so I'm not picking on schools just to be clear the second one is I continue to be frustrated by the lack of communication and steps to get the zoning violation at Centerville high school fixed so I just would like to hear back in writing in an answer to a budget question what is the plan to fix the zoning violation at Centerville high school and that's my two questions and I'll leave it at that okay

supervisor thank you I guess my my question would be just to make sure we all get updates on transit funding in Richmond right now there are two versions. There's a House version of the budget bill and there's a Senate version. One includes capital funding but not operating. The other includes operating but not capital. And this is specific to WMATA where we do have an interstate obligation to that system. So that could put us

in a real pickle depending upon how that turns out. So because we're basically depending upon in the state coming up. They did last, two years ago, one time about $150 million for WMATA. And, you know, Fairfax County portion, a portion of that is about half. So anyway, I would just ask that we all be kept up to date on that. Thank you. Thank you, Supervisor Alcorn. And this is something we're going to continue to track. We track at legislative committee meetings, but as

you mentioned there's also you know there's solutions to the problem this year and then there's solutions to the problem that can put this off and not have this come up every single year to your point earlier and so we've all we have advocated as a board for the permanent solution so that we don't have to fight this battle every year but at a minimum we hope to get through this year with enough funding to fund this year's obligations if they're not going to put the permanent fix in so that we can work on that for next year. And so we're going to continue to monitor that, but without that puts a giant hole in our budget, without a doubt. And the larger

piece, if we're able to get the larger piece, the hope is this funds far more than just Metro, but a lot of other transit operations within the county, which frees up general fund dollars for other obligations, which is really important. Supervisor Stork. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and thank you all very much for being here and appreciate the work that's gone into the budget presentations on all sides.

And I know the challenge we truly have. The challenge we truly have, in my mind, is in Richmond. Not only the JLARC study, which demonstrated that, documented that, $600 million at a minimum, we could argue, really should be coming our way.

And on the county side, just broadly, 50-50, we send a dollar to Richmond, we get 50 cents back. We ought to all be talking about that constantly with our state legislative people because it's real money that doesn't go into the school's pockets or other people's pockets and definitely is coming out of our own residence pockets, and we need to do what we can to address that.

So we have the UVA study that we did to further document that, and if anybody you speak with says, oh, it's not really 50 cents because we do all these other things, no, the Weldon Cooper study did identify all the direct and indirect services that we get from the state, and clearly documented that we get about 50 cents back on the dollar.

So if somebody argues that or says otherwise to you, just ask them if they could please have the state legislature do a study like JLARC, and we'd be happy to monitor and work at that and work with them and see what that would turn out to be. But I think we all know that answer, and that's the answer that I've gotten when I've spoken with some of our state legislative leaders about it.

So we ought to stay focused on the revenue side. On the expense side, we do have to look at how do we reduce our costs where we can, particularly in areas that we know aren't directly in the classroom or directly in the services that we offer and provide to our residents.

I strongly urge you to do something that our county executive has done now. I think this is the fourth year, sir. And, yes, it's, you know, in a huge multibillion-dollar budget, you know, you can look at $35 million and say, well, it's not a whole lot, But if you add up 35 and 35 and 35, you get to a real significant impact, as well as I think you get to a confidence building, as well as you get to a statement to our constituents, our residents, as well as to our employees that we're committed to operating in a very effective, highly efficient organization.

It's tough to make that same argument on the school side. I need, and I'm asking this as a question, I need evidence that I can point to that says schools have done something similar. When our enrollments have declined some, I know our administrative staff, our assistant principals, and a lot of those others, the number of leaders in the schools seems like it's higher than I've observed in the past, at least in my experiences.

So I welcome evidence to the contrary, but I most importantly want the board here to look at those as opportunities to really dig in and make a difference in the school budget and in turn point to residents about how you're making sure you're closing the gaps that are out there, 30, 40, whatever that gap might be with efficiencies and evidence that the schools can operate more effectively but still keep those dollars in the classroom.

So thank you all very much. Supervisor Sizemore Izer. Thank you. And first my apologies my former colleague Ms. Dixit for putting you in the hot seat this year But you know having most recently sat over there in this meeting in the fall and now sitting over here I appreciate the chance to talk and I think the common theme that I'm hearing I think there's a lot of room for collaboration across both boards is that advocacy to the state And it's a really common theme because we've seen from the J. Lark study the underfunding of schools We've seen also, I'm going to say, the uncertainty of this year's budget, both on education funding and on transportation funding.

It's hard to plan if we don't know if that permanent transportation, that's going to be a permanent transportation bucket of funds or if it's going to be a one-year. If it's in the budget, we don't know if it's going to be in the budget again after two years of the biennium. So I think that makes it more difficult for us to address really looking at our strategic priorities from a more stable way of knowing what our budget is going to be, funding is going to be. So I think there's an opportunity there to advocate. And I think part of the message we've got to jointly send to Richmond is I think we all recognize that having a strong transit system, having strong public safety, and having strong schools

is an economic driver of Northern Virginia. It just is, right? And that means that we, if we are strong economically, the state is strong economically. And that's a message we need to get across to tell the state the reason you need to fund JLARC the way it is, the reason we need to have certainty around our transportation funds so we can plan longer-term projects is so we can maintain our economic competitiveness so that we're not choosing, we're not cutting, we're funding services. So I think that's a message that we need to really hone to our communities. I'm just going to say, you know, together we can say to our constituents about

helping our constituents understand why are we in this austere times in the budget, What are the economic signs we're seeing already in Northern Virginia? We talked about this, that we're coming out of this. But how are we hamstrung by the state in not just our longer-term planning, but continue to come out of this economic stage if the state doesn't understand the importance of funding Northern Virginia?

So I think that's a big picture that we can look at from the budget from a communications standpoint. So I'll stop there. Thank you. Supervisor Palczyk. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you to our excellent budget staff and the work you do year-round. I'm excited to have a colleague here.

Sorry, Seema. We love her. And, you know, I think to me it's the conversation we're having here, and I appreciate the tone that's been set, right? We are one Fairfax. We have the same constituents. Our state partners share the same constituents as we do here.

And so, you know, things have changed since I moved here in 1990, a little bit after Mr. Moon, not too long. And, you know, some of the challenges that we have now are different. The cost of living is definitely something that was not there for our families three decades ago.

And so more than ever, we have to look at that and the investments we make. So I think in order to continue this conversation, my ask would be I appreciate the data that's been shared over the past five years for residential and for the changing population of our students.

I would ask, because I think it's important for us to see, but also our constituents, I guess it's a formal ask, is if we could show sort of the line items. Can we break down both the past five years in our projections for residential, what we mean, the different types of residential, put it all in one place, the different types of non-residential, where we've come the last five years?

Because as we hopefully all know watching this, we do not have a local income tax. So real estate is the majority of that local option. But then also for our student, our student population we know has many challenges, and so while the total population may be seeing a decline, a projected decline, it would be helpful to see, because we know that it's there, that the needs of our free and reduced student meals, students on FRM, of our students receiving ESOL services, and our students with disabilities, because we know that the targeted supports there have to differ.

And then, you know, I was having a conversation with one of our state colleagues last week about, he said, well, Daryl from CSBI, I hope he realizes what he's stepping into in Richmond because most, I don't think any other locality is supporting community services boards the way Fairfax County has been doing that.

And that supports all of our kids, all of our families, everyone. So let's focus on the things we do well together and the investment that Fairfax makes out of our own residents' pockets, out of our local funding. And I just hope we can show more of that data of what we are doing as a locality, whether it's going directly to schools or staying in general county services, and why more than ever, we absolutely have to have that partnership.

And finally, we were told for many years, do the meals tax. I was on the school board when we were told, work on it. And we did. Many of us volunteered many hours. And now we have. And I think we need to be very clear. We stepped up to the bat. We know it's not popular, but we knew we needed to diversify our tax base.

And that's pretty much the only diversification tool we have at this point. So I think we need to continue to share that message. And also the fact that, you know, we are all rolling up our sleeves and doing not just on the revenue side and the spending cut side, but on the revenue side, economic development, what do we control, housing costs and priorities, what do we control?

And it is a delta, but I appreciate that we're looking at our shared delta, and we'll keep working together. So I appreciate the shared tenor and the tone. I think that's what our community expects of us. So I appreciate that from our colleagues on the school board. Thank you, Supervisor Palchek, and I'll add on the first part of yours on the real estate piece.

I'm hopeful that all school board members have scheduled a briefing with their counterparts on the Board of Supervisors with our real estate folks so that you can see what's happening on assessments both on commercial and residential in your districts. There are some districts in this county that are performing very well when it comes to commercial growth, And then there are other districts that have no commercial growth.

And so I think it's important for us to see that and to see where that economic development is happening and, frankly, challenge ourselves as to how we can do better countywide in some of those metrics. And so if you do not have one of those scheduled, please reach out to my office.

We'd be happy to set up a second one. I know with the at-large folks, we're going to work on getting those scheduled. But if those are not happening, let me know, because I think it's important context for all of us to know where the revenue is coming from, what's happening with valuations in our communities, who's paying those.

I know I always look every year at the assessment increases disproportionately on the lowest value properties, which is a different question than if they're on the highest value properties in terms of who can afford to pay the increases. So I think those are important things for us all to be looking at.

Supervisor Lusk. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. My comments are just going to be directed at slide four.
